sources.citation: Carrington, Lois & Geraldine Triffitt. 1999. OZBIB: a linguistic bibliography of Aboriginal Australia and the Torres Strait Islands. Pacific Linguistics D-92.
sources.note: Language index for Jurruru/Djururu lists only Austin 1981 (two papers), 1987, 1988 (two papers): no grammar, sketch or phonology of Jurruru had been published by 1999.

sources.citation: Dench, Alan. 1995. Martuthunira: a language of the Pilbara region of Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics C-125 (already held by the project for mart1255).
sources.note: Mentions Jurruru only in classification passages (pp. 5-7); its stress section (2.6) describes Martuthunira, not Jurruru. Context only.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page and full reference list (10 entries) for tjur1240.
sources.note: The single 'grammar'-typed entry is the Thieberger handbook (bibliographic); the rest are overview/comparative papers (Austin 1981, 1988a, 1988b; Dench 1994 pronoun paradigms; Brandenstein 1967; Bowern 2011). None is a description of Jurruru.

sources.citation: Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre website, language and resources pages.
sources.note: Jurruru is not among the languages for which the centre lists any resource.

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas. 1996. Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal Languages South of the Kimberley Region, online edition, section 4.4.3 Jurruru (the source named by the earlier scan).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.W5 T47 1993)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.W5 T47 1993
sources.note: Identical in substance to the print entry: names, classification (Ngayarda), 2 speakers in 1967, none by 1986, 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None'; lists only unpublished materials (O'Grady 1967 vocabulary, Brandenstein 1982 'Tjururu' ts., Dench 1982 fieldnotes, Austin notes). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: AIATSIS AUSTLANG entry W33 Jurruru (the Internet Archive copy, 2023).
sources.note: Documentation table: word list '1?', text collection 'Small (20-100 pages)', grammar '2? (on Mantharta languages)' = Austin 1987 'A reference grammar of the Mantharta languages' ms; dictionary = 'Austin, Peter. Jurruru dictionary, ASEDA 0593'. No stress information.

sources.citation: AIATSIS Audiovisual Archive. 2008. Finding aid VON-BRANDENSTEIN_C04: Sound recordings collected by Carl von Brandenstein, 1967-1970 (24 reels). Canberra: AIATSIS. [Jurruru: field tape 14 (item 002150A, 00:52:50 'Narrative in Jurruru with Bob Williams') and field tape 29 (item 002156A, 'Narratives and language elicitation in Jurruru and Nhanta with Bob Williams and Wardi Barker', Carnarvon, 9 Dec 1968)]
sources.note: No phonology content: a tape inventory. It establishes that connected Jurruru speech and elicitation from one of the last speakers exist on tape at AIATSIS (open for on-site listening; copies at the Archive's discretion) - the only material on which Jurruru stress could ever be measured. Companion finding aids VON-BRANDENSTEIN_C05 and OGRADY_G03 were also read and contain no Jurruru; Austin's P07/P10/P11 finding aids could not be downloaded (web.archive.org refused connections twice).

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas. 2008. Language is like a carpet: Carl-Georg von Brandenstein and Australian languages. In William B. McGregor (ed.), Encountering Aboriginal languages: studies in the history of Australian linguistics, 321-335. Pacific Linguistics 591. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU. (Published version, University of Melbourne Minerva Access, hdl:11343/34254.)
sources.note: No Jurruru language data and nothing on stress, accent or tone in any language. The relevant content is the characterisation of Brandenstein's notation (p. 9): 'he was concerned to use a spelling system based on his view of the etymology of the word.. with the result that the form of a word in his work can not be expected to be a phonemic representation. Further, he used voiced symbols, for example, to contrast their morphological position, thus voiced morpheme-medially but voiceless morpheme-initially', and 'The value of the texts and vocabulary he presented is reduced by the need to deciphe…

sources.citation: Thieberger 1996 online handbook, annotated bibliography pages for Austin, Brandenstein, Dench, O'Grady.
sources.note: Annotations only: Brandenstein 1982 'Tjururu' ts. (AIATSIS A330) = 22-page vocabulary, suffixes, 7 texts; Dench 1982 Jurruru fieldnotes (PALC 200) = 23 pages of sentences and words; Austin 1986 'Southern Pilbara phonology' ts. = 'Discussion of phonological characteristics including stopping of laterals. Includes acoustic data.' No stress statement for Jurruru.

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nick. 1993. Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal languages south of the Kimberley region. Pacific Linguistics C-124. Canberra: ANU. Jurruru entry 4.4.3, pp. 109-111; pronunciation guide sec. 1.5.1, p. 6.
sources.note: Jurruru entry is purely bibliographic ('9. Grammar or sketch grammar: None'; no phoneme inventory, no stress). The only stress remark is region-wide, in the pronunciation guide p. 6: 'Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest' — a generalisation over all WA languages, not a statement about Jurruru.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1988. Aboriginal languages of the Gascoyne-Ashburton region. La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics 1: 43-63.
sources.note: Language-situation overview and annotated bibliography. On Jurruru: 'There are three sources for Jurruru, vocabulary collected by G. N. O'Grady in 1967, sentences and texts collected by C. G. von Brandenstein from the same person, and sentences collected by Austin and Dench from the Jiwarli informant, who had learnt Jurruru as a child.' No phonology, no stress (the word 'stress' occurs only as 'distressed').

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1988. Classification of Southern Pilbara languages. Papers in Australian Linguistics 17, 1-17. Pacific Linguistics A-71. doi:10.15144/PL-A71.1
sources.note: Lexicostatistic and morphological classification; Jurruru placed in Ngayarta on the basis of notes from Dench and Brandenstein. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1988. Phonological voicing contrasts in Australian Aboriginal languages. La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics 1: 17-42.
sources.note: Mentions stress only in quotations about other languages (e.g. Breen on Arandic); Jurruru not mentioned.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1983. Southern Pilbara dictionaries. In Peter Austin (ed.), Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 15: Australian Aboriginal lexicography, 1-17. Pacific Linguistics A-66. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-A66.1
sources.note: Lexicography-project description. Phonological content limited to the practical orthography shared by all project languages: laminals th/nh/lh, retroflexes rt/rn/rl, voiceless stop symbols (voiced only for Tharrkari and Purduna), 'three phonemic vowels - i, u, a and phonemic length; long vowels are written double'. Jurruru entries carry O'Grady's 1966 proto-Ngayarta etyma (patha-nma 'throw' < *patha-R, warnpi-nma 'hit' < *warnpi-L). No mention of stress or accent anywhere.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter. 1981. Proto-Kanyara and proto-Mantharta historical phonology. Lingua 54: 295-333.
sources.note: Segmental reconstruction of Kanyara and Mantharta only; no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent'; Jurruru not treated in the text (Glottolog tags it for Jurruru only because Austin then classified Jurruru as Mantharta, a classification he later withdrew).

sources.citation: Brandenstein, C. G. von. 1967. The language situation in the Pilbara - past and present. In C. G. von Brandenstein, A. Capell & K. Hale (eds), Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 2, 1-20 (+ maps). Pacific Linguistics A-11. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-A11.1
sources.note: No phonology of Tjururu. Geographic/typological survey: name etymology (Tjururu = 'Lowlanders'), placement in the 'intermediate belt' (Njamal, Pandjima, Tjururu, Wadjarri) between AVC coastal and PVC inland verb-conjugation types, population <=2. The only stress remark in the paper (p. c. 9) concerns Jindjiparndi: in fast speech 'only the shift of stress from the first syllable will reveal vowel length' after medial-stop lenition - not about Tjururu.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Jurruru language' (rev. 1343671717).
sources.note: Grammar notes taken from Austin 1988 and Austin's 2015 Mantharta grammar ms; no phonology section, nothing on stress.
